content: The combination of emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide (AF) is indicated for use with other antiretroviral agents (ARTs) in the treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults. The recommended dosage is 200 mg/25 mg taken orally once daily. It is also indicated for at-risk patients to reduce the risk of HIV-1 infection from sexual exposure, excluding those at risk from receptive vaginal sex, with the same dosage of 200 mg/25 mg orally once daily. For specific dosing recommendations when co-administering third agents for HIV treatment, refer to their respective prescribing information or AIDSinfo guidelines. For at-risk adolescents weighing ≥35 kg, emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (AF) is indicated to reduce the risk of HIV-1 infection from sexual exposure, excluding those at risk from receptive vaginal sex. The recommended dosage for adolescents weighing ≥35 kg is 200 mg/25 mg orally once daily. Safety and efficacy have not been established for adolescents weighing <35 kg. For specific dosing recommendations for co-administered third agents for HIV treatment, refer to their respective prescribing information or AIDSinfo guidelines. Drug Interactions: 1. Enasidenib: Enasidenib increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by mechanisms involving other pathways. Avoid co-administration with sensitive OATP1B1, OATP1B3, or BCRP substrates, as minimal concentration changes may lead to serious toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the substrate dosage according to its prescribing information. 2. Leniolisib: Leniolisib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by increasing systemic exposure of BCRP substrates. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 3. Letermovir: Tenofovir AF decreases the level or effect of letermovir via P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. Co-administration of letermovir with P-gp inducers is not recommended. 4. Sotorasib: Sotorasib decreases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If use is unavoidable, refer to the prescribing information of the P-gp substrate for dosage modifications. 5. Tepotinib: Tepotinib increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Avoid or use an alternative drug. If concomitant use is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage if recommended in its approved product labeling. 6. Acalabrutinib: Acalabrutinib increases the level of tenofovir AF by inhibiting intestinal BCRP. Use caution and monitor closely for increased exposure to co-administered BCRP substrates. 7. Apalutamide: Apalutamide decreases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by increasing elimination. It weakly induces BCRP and may decrease systemic exposure of BCRP substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Berotralstat: Berotralstat increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Monitor or titrate the P-gp substrate dose if co-administered. 9. Cabozantinib: Tenofovir AF increases the level or effect of cabozantinib by mechanisms involving other pathways. Use caution and monitor closely. MRP2 inhibitors increase cabozantinib toxicity. 10. Danicopan: Danicopan increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. It increases plasma concentrations of P-gp substrates. Consider dose reduction of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious adverse reactions. 11. Darolutamide: Darolutamide, a BCRP inhibitor, increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF. Avoid co-administration with BCRP inhibitors. If use is unavoidable, closely monitor for adverse reactions and consider dose reduction of BCRP substrate drugs. 12. Duvelisib: Tenofovir AF decreases the level or effect of duvelisib via P-gp efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Elagolix: Elagolix increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Encorafenib: Encorafenib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases the concentration and toxicities of BCRP substrates. Closely monitor for signs and symptoms of increased exposure and consider adjusting the dose of these substrates. 15. Fostamatinib: Fostamatinib increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by decreasing metabolism. Concomitant use may increase concentrations of BCRP substrate drugs. Monitor for toxicities of BCRP substrate drugs that may require dosage reduction. 16. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: This combination increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by decreasing metabolism. It may increase plasma concentration of BCRP substrates. Use caution and monitor closely. 17. Ifosfamide: Ifosfamide and tenofovir AF may increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Monitor electrolytes and renal function closely. 18. Istradefylline: Istradefylline increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Clinical trials have shown increased peak levels and AUC of P-gp substrates. Consider dose reduction of sensitive P-gp substrates. 19. Lonafarnib: Lonafarnib, a weak P-gp inhibitor, increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Monitor for adverse reactions if co-administered with P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities. Reduce P-gp substrate dose if needed. 20. Mavorixafor: Mavorixafor increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Exercise caution if co-administered with a sensitive P-gp substrate where minimal substrate concentration changes may lead to serious adverse effects. 21. Momelotinib: Momelotinib, a BCRP inhibitor, increases the toxicity of tenofovir AF by plasma protein binding competition. It may increase exposure of BCRP substrates, raising the risk of adverse reactions. Dose adjustment of other BCRP substrates may be necessary. 22. Nirmatrelvir: Nirmatrelvir increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration may increase tenofovir systemic exposures. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Orlistat: Orlistat decreases the level or effect of tenofovir AF by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Loss of virological control has been reported in HIV-infected patients taking orlistat concomitantly. Monitor HIV RNA levels frequently, and if increased viral load is confirmed, discontinue orlistat. 24. Otesaconazole: Otesaconazole, a BCRP inhibitor, increases the effects and risk of toxicities of BCRP substrates. Use the lowest starting dose of BCRP substrates or consider reducing their dose. 25. Regorafenib: Regorafenib likely inhibits BCRP transport, increasing systemic exposure to BCRP substrates and related toxicity. Monitor closely and consider therapy modification. 26. Safinamide: Safinamide and its major metabolite may inhibit intestinal BCRP, increasing the level or effect of tenofovir AF. Monitor BCRP substrates for increased pharmacologic or adverse effects. 27. Sarecycline: Sarecycline increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Monitor for toxicities of P-gp substrates that may require dosage reduction when co-administered with P-gp inhibitors. 28. Stiripentol: Stiripentol, a BCRP transport inhibitor, increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF. Consider dosage reduction for BCRP substrates if adverse effects are experienced when co-administered. 29. Tafamidis: Tafamidis inhibits breast cancer resistant protein (BCRP) in vitro and may increase exposure of BCRP substrates following tafamidis or tafamidis meglumine administration. Dosage adjustment of these BCRP substrates may be necessary. 30. Tucatinib: Tucatinib increases the level or effect of tenofovir AF via P-gp efflux transporter. Consider reducing the dosage of P-gp substrates where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities. 31. Vadadustat: Vadadustat may increase exposure of BCRP substrates. Monitor for signs of adverse effects of BCRP substrates and reduce substrate dose in accordance with their product labeling. 32. Voclosporin: Voclosporin and tenofovir AF may increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk for acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. Monitor closely.
